title: Triage a work-order queue in fifteen minutes
mechanism_check: Life-safety first: active water, no heat in winter, failed security doors, and anything blocking egress outrank everything.
Occupied vs vacant: a broken fixture in an occupied patient room or classroom beats the same failure in storage.
Find the blockers: one ticket that unblocks three others (a tripped main, a dead air handler) jumps the line.
Check the clock: a ticket aging past its SLA is about to become someone else's emergency.
improvised_tools: A 2x2 urgent/important grid sketched on paper or a whiteboard
Colored tape dots on a printed queue: red = today, yellow = this week, none = scheduled
A 15-minute timer so triage never turns into doing the work
steps: Dump every open ticket into one view; anything older than 7 days gets flagged regardless of priority.
Tag life-safety and occupant-impact tickets red. These are today's work, no debate.
Tag blockers: tickets whose fix unblocks other tickets move up with them.
Batch by zone: group nearby tickets so one trip covers several fixes.
Commit to today's top five in writing; everything else gets a real date, not 'soon'.
Report the queue honestly upward: what got done, what's waiting, and what's blocking.
stop_conditions: Never re-prioritize a life-safety ticket below convenience work to please a loud requester.
Never close a ticket you did not personally verify as fixed.
If the queue grows faster than the crew clears it for three shifts running, escalate the staffing gap in writing -- triage cannot fix understaffing.

title: Read a building with a walk-through survey
mechanism_check: Buildings announce failures early: stains on ceiling tiles, the sound of running water with no tap open, hot electrical smells, doors that stopped latching.
Walk the same route in the same order every time; change is what you are hunting, and change only shows against a baseline.
Ceiling-to-floor scan: most institutional failures start above the ceiling or below the floor and surface in the middle.
improvised_tools: Phone camera: photograph every anomaly with the room number visible in the frame
A small notebook dated per walk, or dated voice memos
Phone flashlight for above-ceiling and under-sink checks
steps: Pick your route: mechanical rooms, restrooms, corridors, stairwells, exterior walls. Same route, weekly.
Scan ceiling, walls, floor in that order; listen for water, hum, and alarms you have tuned out.
Photograph anything new: stains, cracks, corrosion, standing water, propped fire doors.
Log it same-day with location and date; a photo with no location is a rumor.
Compare week to week: growing stains and spreading corrosion become work orders before they become emergencies.
stop_conditions: Do not lift ceiling tiles in patient-care, food-prep, or clean areas without that area's infection-control protocol -- in hospitals this is an ICRA line.
In correctional or secured facilities, never enter a housing or restricted area unescorted to 'just look'.
If you find asbestos-suspect material (old pipe insulation, 9-inch floor tile) damaged or disturbed: stop, do not touch it, report it. Asbestos work is licensed-only.

title: Write a work order the next tech can actually fix
mechanism_check: Vague tickets waste trips: 'bathroom broken' sends a tech to the wrong floor with the wrong parts.
A fixable ticket has five fields: exact location, observed symptom, when it started, access constraints, and who to contact.
Report symptoms, not diagnoses: 'water on floor under sink, started this morning' beats 'pipe burst' when it is actually a supply line sweating.
improvised_tools: The building's room-numbering convention (learn it; 'the big conference room' is not a location)
One annotated photo attached to the ticket: circle the problem
The requester's name and a callback number, not just a department
steps: Write the exact location first: building, floor, room number, and position in the room.
Describe what you see/hear/smell and when it started. No theories.
Note access: locked room, occupied hours, patient area, need for escort.
Attach the annotated photo and the callback contact.
Set an honest priority: safety, occupant impact, or routine -- and say why in one line.
stop_conditions: Never mark a ticket urgent to jump the queue; false urgency trains everyone to ignore the flag.
Never assign the fix to a specific person by name in the ticket unless that is your authority.
If the symptom suggests a life-safety system (alarm, sprinkler, egress), call it in by phone too -- do not rely on the ticket queue alone.

title: Run a clean shift handoff
mechanism_check: The handoff is where institutional knowledge dies: an unlogged temp fix becomes the next shift's mystery failure.
Ten structured minutes beats two hours of rework and one angry occupant.
The incoming shift cannot act on what they cannot repeat back; the test of a handoff is repetition, not politeness.
improvised_tools: A handoff log or board with three columns: active jobs, watch items, parts on order
Voice memo recorded while walking the live jobs, sent to the group
The 'three alive' ritual: three things still alive when you leave, named out loud
steps: Outgoing writes first: update the log before talking, while the details are fresh.
Incoming reads first, then asks questions; never hand off verbally with no written record.
Walk the live jobs together when they matter: point at the temp fix, the open panel, the tagged valve.
Name an owner for every open item, including the ones waiting on parts.
Sign the log. A signed handoff is a contract; an unsigned one is a rumor.
stop_conditions: Never accept a handoff you cannot repeat back in your own words.
Never hand off an unverified temporary fix as if it were a permanent repair.
If the outgoing tech is gone before you arrive, do not assume the log is complete -- verify the watch items yourself.

title: Map your building's shutoffs in one walk
mechanism_check: In a water or gas emergency you get one calm walk now or one panicked search later; the map is the difference.
Every building has layers: main shutoffs, zone valves, and fixture stops. Know all three, in order.
Some valves you must know but never touch: fire and medical-gas valves are look-don't-touch.
improvised_tools: Painter's tape and marker for temporary labels that survive until the engraved tags arrive
Phone photos of every valve and panel with the location in the frame
A sketched floor plan if no printed one exists -- hand-drawn beats nothing
steps: Walk with someone who knows the building; record water main, zone valves, and fixture stops.
Record electrical panels and what each actually feeds (verify the directory; directories lie).
Locate the gas shutoff, the fire alarm panel, and medical-gas zone valves -- note them as look-don't-touch.
Label everything with tape and marker; photograph the labeled set.
File the map where the on-call tech can reach it at 2am, and hand a copy to your supervisor.
stop_conditions: Never operate a fire alarm panel, sprinkler valve, or medical-gas zone valve -- locate and label only; those belong to licensed contractors and authorized staff.
Never close a valve if you do not know what is downstream of it and whether you can reopen it.
Never force a stuck shutoff with a cheater bar; a snapped valve stem turns a leak into a flood.

title: Improvise a temporary fix that will not lie to the next shift
mechanism_check: Temporary fixes are honest when labeled and scheduled; an unlabeled temp fix becomes the next failure and the next tech's trap.
Choose reversible: tape, clamps, and shims come off cleanly; drilled holes and cut pipes do not.
A temp fix buys time for the real repair -- it is never the repair.
improvised_tools: Red tags with zip ties: TEMP, date, your name, and what the real fix needs
The 48-hour rule: every temp fix gets a real-fix date within 48 hours or it becomes the top priority
Phone photo of the temp fix attached to the work order
steps: Diagnose first: a temp fix on the wrong problem is just damage with a label.
Pick the most reversible method that holds safely: clamp over weld, shim over cut, tape over bypass.
Tag it red: TEMP + date + your name + parts needed for the permanent fix.
Log it in the handoff and the work order with a photo; say it out loud at shift change.
Schedule the permanent repair before you leave; a temp fix with no date is a permanent lie.
stop_conditions: Temporary fixes never touch life-safety systems: no temp wiring on emergency circuits, no propped fire doors, no bypassed interlocks.
Never leave an unlabeled temporary fix anywhere in the building.
If the temp fix cannot hold safely until the scheduled repair date, escalate now -- do not stretch it.

title: Stock a shift kit that covers eighty percent of calls
mechanism_check: Most institutional calls are the same dozen failures: running toilets, dead outlets, loose hardware, drips, burnt lamps, tripped breakers.
Carrying the fix beats a parts run across a 400,000-square-foot campus every time.
A kit you will not carry is decoration: weight and size decide whether it rides along.
improvised_tools: A 5-gallon bucket or tool bag as the carrier -- cheap, replaceable, fits in a cart
The dozen: tape, zip ties, pliers, multi-bit driver, flashlight + batteries, fuses, valve washers, door shims, caulk, rags, gloves
A restock card taped inside the lid: used it, replace it, same shift
steps: Audit last month's tickets and list the ten most common failures.
Kit the fix for each: the part plus the tool to install it.
Assemble the carrier; if you cannot lift it with one hand, cut it down.
Tape the restock card inside the lid and follow it: used = replaced the same shift.
Review quarterly: the building changes, and the kit must change with it.
stop_conditions: The kit never carries bypasses: no cheater plugs, no jumper wires for safeties, no taped fuses.
Never pull a safety device (fuse, breaker, GFCI) from the kit's donor pile -- safeties are bought new.
If the kit is empty of a stocked item twice in one week, the stocking list is wrong -- fix the list, not the tech.

title: Navigate the chain of command to get a fix approved
mechanism_check: Institutions run on signatures: know whose signature unlocks spending, space access, and schedule changes.
Approvers decide on risk and cost, not on craft: speak their language -- dollars, downtime, liability.
The cost of waiting is your strongest argument: a $200 bearing today is a $20,000 motor next month.
improvised_tools: A mental org chart: who owns the budget, who owns the space, who owns the calendar
The one-page ask: problem, cost, risk of waiting, the ask -- one page, no more
A dated photo of the failure; paper persuades, photos compel
steps: Identify the budget owner for the system, not just your supervisor.
Write the one-pager: problem in one line, cost, what happens if you wait, the specific ask.
Bring the photo and, if you can, the failed part.
Get the approval in writing -- email counts; a nod in the hallway does not.
Thank the signer and report back when the fix lands; approvers fund people who close the loop.
stop_conditions: Never spend money you were not authorized to spend, even if the fix is obviously needed.
Never go around your supervisor to their boss first -- inform up the chain in order.
If the approver says no in writing, stop and document it; the liability for the delay is now theirs, on record.

title: Log your work so the next tech trusts it
mechanism_check: Your log is your reputation in a building that outlasts your shift; techs trust logs, not legends.
Five lines beat five paragraphs: found, did, used, still open, name + time.
The 'still open' line is the most valuable: it tells the next tech exactly where you stopped.
improvised_tools: Ticket comments with before/after photos
A parts-used line: part name, source (stock, donor, purchased), and quantity
Timestamp and name on every entry -- anonymous logs are rumors
steps: Write what you found, in symptoms: what was broken, what it looked like.
Write what you did, in verbs: tightened, replaced, reset, cleaned.
Write what you used: parts, and where they came from.
Write what is still open: the follow-up, the part on order, the temp fix with its date.
Sign with name and time. Done.
stop_conditions: Never log work you did not do, including 'verified' on someone else's repair.
Never skip the 'still open' line to make a ticket look clean.
If you cannot remember what you did, say so and re-inspect -- a guessed log is worse than a thin one.

title: Escalate without crying wolf
mechanism_check: Escalation is a currency: spend it on real emergencies and it keeps its value; spend it on routine and nobody answers when it matters.
The three-question test: is it a safety issue, is it spreading, is it beyond my authority? Two yeses = escalate.
Escalate with facts and a proposed next move, not with alarm.
improvised_tools: The written trail: ticket note, email, or log entry with time and facts
A photo that shows scale: a coin next to the crack, a hand next to the stain
Your supervisor's preferred escalation channel -- learn it before the emergency
steps: Work it at your level first and document the attempt.
Apply the three-question test; if it passes, escalate now, not after one more try.
Call up with facts: what, where, since when, what you tried, what you propose.
Follow up in writing so the escalation exists outside the phone call.
Stay on it until someone with authority owns it; escalation is a handoff, not a throw.
stop_conditions: Never escalate by texting a photo with no context.
Never skip your supervisor in a non-emergency to reach their boss.
In a true emergency (fire, major water, injury): call emergency services first, the chain of command second.

title: Diagnose a commercial restroom drain backup
mechanism_check: Backups have three causes: local blockage (one fixture), venting failure (gurgling, slow drains), or a main-line problem (multiple fixtures backing up). Diagnose before you plunge.
One fixture affected = your problem. Multiple fixtures on the same branch = the building's problem, upstream of you.
Flush valves and floor drains share lines: check both before deciding where the blockage sits.
improvised_tools: A closet auger for the toilet; a plunger for the lavatory -- never the reverse
A bucket and gloves to bail the bowl before augering
Phone light to read the cleanout and check for standing water in the line
steps: Test every fixture in the restroom: note which back up and which drain fine.
If one fixture is affected, bail it down and auger or plunge that fixture only.
If multiple fixtures back up, find the cleanout and check for standing water -- that means the blockage is downstream.
Clear what is local; report a main-line blockage upward with the cleanout reading.
Disinfect the area and verify flow at every fixture before closing the ticket.
stop_conditions: Never use chemical drain cleaner in an institution: liability, pipe damage, and a hazard for the next tech who opens the line.
Multiple-fixture backup with standing water at the cleanout = call it in; do not snake a main blind.
If sewage is involved rather than grey water, switch to the sewage protocol (institutional-030) -- different PPE, different vac.

title: Contain a roof leak when you cannot touch the roof
mechanism_check: You cannot fix the roof from inside, but you can control where the water goes -- containment is the whole job.
Water travels: the drip you see is rarely under the breach; trace upward and outward to the highest wet point.
A string wicks water silently into a bucket; a bucket alone under a drip splashes and spreads.
improvised_tools: Tarps and plastic sheeting to protect what is below
String or yarn tied at the drip point, hanging into a bucket -- the wick method
Wet-floor signs and barrier tape; a leak zone with no signs is a slip lawsuit
steps: Trace the water to its highest interior point; photograph the trail for the roofer.
Move or cover everything valuable under the path: equipment, records, electronics.
Tie a wick string at the drip point into a bucket; place tarps under the whole zone.
Sign and barrier the area; wet floors in corridors need signs at both approaches.
Log the leak with photos and call the roofing contractor or supervisor -- your containment holds the line until they arrive.
stop_conditions: Never go on the roof without fall protection and authorization -- OSHA's line, not yours to cross.
Never puncture a ceiling to 'let it drain' in occupied space without approval; water plus hidden electrical is a shock risk.
If water is entering an electrical room or panel area, kill power to the area (authorized person) and escalate immediately.

title: Free a stuck flush valve in a high-traffic restroom
mechanism_check: Flush valves stick from debris or scale on the diaphragm or piston; the water must be off before you open anything.
The stop valve (the screwdriver slot on the side) is your friend -- and your risk: old stops snap.
Diaphragm kits are cheap and standardized; carry the two common sizes.
improvised_tools: Adjustable wrench and a screwdriver for the stop and the cap
Spare diaphragm kit in the two common sizes
Bucket and towels: the valve body holds water even with the stop closed
steps: Close the stop valve gently; flush once to relieve pressure.
Remove the cap, lift the diaphragm assembly, and rinse it clean; inspect the seat for nicks.
Replace the diaphragm if it is torn, stiff, or scaled beyond cleaning.
Reassemble, open the stop slowly, and test-flush twice, watching for weeping at the cap.
If it holds, log the part used; restock the kit the same shift.
stop_conditions: If the stop valve will not turn or starts leaking when touched, stop -- a snapped stop floods the chase. Call it in.
Never force brass fittings with a cheater bar; brass yields suddenly and then you own a flood.
If the valve body itself is cracked, do not patch it -- replace the valve.

title: Reset a tripped breaker in an institution without guessing
mechanism_check: A breaker trips for a reason: overload, short, or ground fault. Resetting blind is how fires start.
Panel directories lie: verify which breaker feeds the dead area with a tester, not the label.
The two-trip rule: one reset to test, a second trip means the circuit stays off and the problem gets diagnosed.
improvised_tools: Non-contact voltage tester to verify dead before touching anything near the panel
Flashlight; panel rooms are always dark when you need them lit
A red tag for the breaker if it must stay off
steps: Identify the tripped breaker: handle sitting between ON and OFF, or flagged by the directory.
Unplug or switch off loads on that circuit before touching the breaker.
Reset once: push fully OFF, then fully ON. If it holds, add loads back one at a time to find the culprit.
If it trips again, leave it OFF, tag it red, and write the ticket for diagnosis.
Log what was on the circuit when it tripped; the pattern is the diagnosis.
stop_conditions: Never reset a breaker more than twice; a repeat trip is a fault, not a nuisance.
Never open a panel interior, replace a breaker, or work live -- licensed electrician only, no exceptions.
Buzzing, burning smell, or heat at the panel = leave it off, clear the area, call the electrician and your supervisor now.

title: Quiet a rattling door closer before replacement
mechanism_check: Closers rattle from three causes: loose arm or bracket screws, low oil (a weeping closer is a dying closer), or a bent arm from abuse.
Tighten and adjust before replacing: most 'dead' closers are just loose.
A closer that cannot control the door's speed is a safety device failing -- treat it accordingly.
improvised_tools: Screwdriver and Allen-key set for arm and bracket screws
Threadlocker on screws that keep backing out from vibration
Shims for a bracket pulling away from a soft frame
steps: Tighten every arm and bracket screw; check the bracket against the frame for flex.
Inspect for oil weeping at the seals; weeping means the closer's days are numbered -- order the replacement now.
Adjust sweep and latch speed so the door closes firmly without slamming.
Shim any bracket that rocks; apply threadlocker to chronic loose screws.
Test the door ten times; a closer that behaves nine times out of ten still needs replacement.
stop_conditions: Fire-rated doors: never disable, remove, or prop open a closer on a fire door (NFPA 80). A de-closered fire door is a code violation and a personal liability.
If the closer body is cracked or the spring is broken, stop adjusting and replace it.
Never substitute a non-rated closer on a fire-rated door -- the rating is the whole point.

title: Run a huddle when the shift is two people short
mechanism_check: A short crew wins by shrinking the mission, not by running faster; exhaustion creates the next emergency.
Split by zone, not by task: two people crisscrossing the building waste the day in transit.
The buddy check is load-bearing: hourly contact is how a short crew stays a team instead of two solo acts.
improvised_tools: The top-five list, cut ruthlessly to life-safety and occupant impact
A 5-minute stand-up at shift start: who takes which zone, what is deferred, who calls for help
Hourly check-in by radio or text; silence past the hour means someone goes looking
steps: Cut the list: life-safety and occupant-impact only. Everything else gets a date and a note.
Split the building into zones, one per person; pair up only for heavy, high, or awkward work.
Set the check-in rhythm: hourly contact, no exceptions.
Call for help early on anything that needs two people or a ladder -- pride is not a tool.
Hand off what is left cleanly: the next shift inherits a short list, not a mystery.
stop_conditions: Never work solo at height, on a roof, or in a confined space to 'make up' for the missing crew.
Never skip the handoff because the shift was brutal; that is when it matters most.
If calls keep coming and the crew cannot cover safely, escalate to supervision -- the schedule is their problem to solve, not yours to absorb.

title: Coordinate a flood response across shifts
mechanism_check: Water wins by spreading; the team wins by dividing the building into owned zones faster than the water divides itself.
Stop the source first, protect the critical rooms second, mop third. Mopping before the source is found is theater.
Critical rooms have an order: electrical rooms, IT/server rooms, records, then everything else.
improvised_tools: A zone map with owner names written on it, posted where everyone can see
Towels, squeegees, and every wet vac the building owns; one runner fetching supplies so the crews never leave their zones
Sandbags or rolled towels at door thresholds to steer water away from critical rooms
steps: Find and stop the source using the shutoff map; if you cannot find it in five minutes, call for help while containing.
Protect critical rooms first: power down what must be powered down (authorized person), move what can be moved, barrier the doors.
Divide the wet area into zones with a named owner per zone; post the map.
Rotate the wet-vac crews; wet work exhausts people fast and tired people get hurt.
Log damage with photos for insurance and the work order; water damage claims live or die on documentation.
stop_conditions: Water in an electrical room or around panels: kill power to the area (authorized person) and wait for clearance -- standing water plus electricity kills.
Sewage water is not flood water: switch to the sewage protocol (institutional-030) with full PPE.
If the source is a sprinkler or fire-suppression line, do not improvise the repair -- contain, call the fire-protection contractor, and notify the fire alarm monitoring company.

title: Build a parts-cannibalization board for your shop
mechanism_check: Institutions retire equipment but landfill the parts with it; a labeled donor shelf beats a purchase order that takes three weeks.
Tested and tagged beats a mystery bin: an untested donor part is a second service call waiting to happen.
The board is a commons: sign-out keeps it honest, and honesty keeps it stocked.
improvised_tools: Shelving and bins claimed from decommissioned areas
Tags: donor equipment, date pulled, what was tested and what passed
A multimeter and basic test rig to verify pulls before they go on the board
steps: Claim decommissioned equipment before it hits the dumpster; get permission in writing from whoever owns the asset.
Strip reusable parts: motors, contactors, valves, handles, fasteners, lenses.
Test every electrical or mechanical part before shelving it; tag the test result.
Tag everything: donor, date, what it fits. Log the board in the shop bible.
Run a sign-out sheet: who took what, for which ticket. Restock from the next retirement.
stop_conditions: Never cannibalize from life-safety equipment: pulling a detector, strobe, or extinguisher part creates a gap in protection.
Never reuse a safety device from a donor -- fuses, breakers, GFCIs, and relief valves are bought new, always.
If the asset owner will not release the equipment in writing, walk away; 'everyone does it' is not authorization.

title: Diagnose a hot-cold complaint in a zoned HVAC building
mechanism_check: Comfort complaints come in three layers: thermostat (setpoint, mode, dead batteries), airflow (blocked vents, closed dampers), or zone (VAV box, failed actuator). Check in that order.
Verify with a thermometer, not feelings: 'freezing' at 72 degrees is a different problem than 62 degrees.
Report the zone, not the room: the fix lives upstream of the complaint.
improvised_tools: A thermometer you trust, carried in the kit
Access to the thermostat and the room's supply vents
Knowledge of which VAV box or zone damper serves the room -- ask the BAS tech or find the as-builts
steps: Measure the room temperature; compare to setpoint and to adjacent rooms.
Check the thermostat: setpoint, mode (heat/cool/auto), and batteries.
Check the supply vent: is air moving, and is it the right temperature?
Trace to the zone: find the VAV box or damper serving the room; check for a failed actuator or a damper stuck shut.
Check for blocked returns: furniture against a return grille starves the whole zone.
Report the zone and the finding; request the BAS or HVAC tech if it is past your level.
stop_conditions: Never open sealed ductwork or touch refrigerant lines -- EPA 608 certification is the legal line.
Never change a building automation setpoint beyond your written authority; log the request instead.
If you find a failed smoke detector or damper interlock tied to the air handler, stop and report -- that is life-safety territory.

title: Light a dark corridor on inspection day
mechanism_check: Darkness reads as neglect to an inspector and as danger to occupants; safe temporary light buys time until the real repair.
The dead circuit is the real problem and gets its own priority ticket; the temp lighting is the bridge.
Cords are the hazard you introduce while solving the darkness: manage them or trade one violation for another.
improvised_tools: LED work lights on stands, run along the wall -- never across the walkway
Cord covers or gaffer tape at every crossing point
Battery lanterns for spots cords cannot reach safely
steps: Identify the dead circuit and write the real repair ticket first -- temp lighting never replaces the work order.
Run corded LED lights along the wall base, secured so they cannot tip into the walkway.
Tape or cover every inch of cord in a traffic path; battery lanterns where cords cannot go.
Verify egress paths stay clear and lit to code minimums; emergency lighting circuits are separate -- check those too.
Log the temp setup with a removal date tied to the permanent repair.
stop_conditions: Cords across an egress path are a trip hazard and a fire-code violation -- reroute or do not deploy.
Temporary lighting is measured in days, not months; if the permanent fix stalls, re-escalate rather than normalize the temp.
Never wire a permanent fixture or circuit yourself -- licensed electrician and permit, no exceptions.

title: Respond to a frozen pipe before it bursts
mechanism_check: Ice expands and splits pipe at the weakest point, usually at a fitting; the burst often happens during the thaw, not the freeze.
Thaw from the faucet side back toward the ice: trapped steam and pressure between the heat and the ice is what bursts pipes.
The freeze point is the coldest section -- feel along the run; frost on the outside marks the spot.
improvised_tools: A hair dryer or heat gun on low -- gentle, movable heat
Towels soaked in hot water wrapped around the frozen section
A space heater to warm the room or chase after the thaw, plus the shutoff map in hand
steps: Open the faucet slightly: flowing water, even a trickle, helps the thaw and relieves pressure.
Locate the shutoff for that run and make sure it works before you start -- if the pipe is already split, you will need it fast.
Warm the pipe gently starting at the faucet side, moving back toward the frozen section; keep the heat moving.
Watch for the drip that becomes a stream: flow restored means the ice is clearing.
Inspect the whole run for splits as it thaws; insulate the section after, and find why it froze (failed heat tape, open vent, dead zone).
stop_conditions: Never use an open flame on a pipe: fire risk, and concentrated heat can flash steam and burst the pipe.
If the pipe is already split, stop thawing, shut the water, and call it in -- thawing a split pipe just feeds the leak.
Never leave a space heater running unattended in a chase or near combustibles to 'keep it thawed'.

title: Move heavy equipment with two people and no forklift
mechanism_check: Heavy moves are about friction and leverage, not strength: rollers, dollies, and pry bars move what backs cannot.
Plan the route before touching the load: measure every door, elevator, and turn; the move fails at the tightest point.
A spotter walking ahead is not optional -- they see what the carriers cannot.
improvised_tools: Furniture dollies, a pry bar, and steel pipes as rollers for flat floors
Lifting straps to keep backs straight and loads stable
Plywood sheets to protect soft floors and bridge thresholds
steps: Measure the load, the route, and every choke point; clear the path completely.
Lay plywood over soft flooring and across thresholds.
Lift with legs and straps onto the dolly or rollers; never twist under load.
Move slowly with the spotter ahead calling obstacles; reposition rollers as you go.
Set the load down on blocks, not on fingers; verify it is stable before letting go.
stop_conditions: Over roughly 100 pounds per person without mechanical help: stop and get more people or a lift.
Never stand or walk under a suspended or tipping load, even 'for a second'.
Back injuries end careers: if the lift feels wrong, set it down and request proper equipment -- no heroics.

title: Handle a lock change when the locksmith is booked out
mechanism_check: Most institutional lockouts are a failed cylinder or a lost key; a cylinder swap is a stopgap, not a rekey of the system.
Institutional key control is a hierarchy: one wrong cylinder in a master-keyed system can break the whole building's keying.
Authorization first: a work order plus supervisor approval, because you are changing who can enter a space.
improvised_tools: Screwdriver set and a replacement cylinder in the same keyway
The key-control log: every cylinder change gets recorded
The failed cylinder, bagged and handed to the locksmith -- evidence beats description
steps: Verify authorization: written work order and supervisor approval before touching the hardware.
Remove the interior hardware and swap the cylinder for the same keyway; never force the keyway.
Test the new key at least three times from both sides; test that the old key no longer works.
Log the change in the key-control record: door, date, cylinder, key issued to whom.
Bag the old cylinder and hand it to the locksmith on their next visit for the permanent rekey.
stop_conditions: Never duplicate a master or restricted-keyway key, and never rekey a master-keyed system yourself -- that breaks the institutional key hierarchy.
Check facility policy first: some institutions forbid any non-locksmith cylinder work; policy is the line.
If the door is a fire-rated door, the hardware must stay rated -- no substitutions that void the listing.

title: Build your promotion case from work-order data
mechanism_check: Promotions go to people with receipts; your ticket history is your resume inside the institution.
Supervisors promote on three things: reliability (shows up, closes tickets), scope (handles harder work), and judgment (knows when to stop).
Ask what the next level requires before you build the case -- every institution's ladder is different.
improvised_tools: Six months of your ticket history: count, first-trip fixes, emergencies owned
The thank-yous: saved emails and notes from occupants and supervisors
The one-page case: numbers on top, examples below, the ask at the end
steps: Pull your last six months of tickets; count total, first-trip fixes, and after-hours emergencies you owned.
List the three hardest jobs you handled and what made them hard.
Collect the written thank-yous; ask two supervisors for specific feedback you can quote.
Ask your supervisor directly: what does the next level require, and where am I short?
Write the one-page case, present it at review time, and ask for the gap-closing plan in writing.
stop_conditions: Never inflate numbers your supervisor can check in the system -- credibility is the whole case.
Never campaign against a coworker to lift yourself; it poisons the team you want to lead.
If the answer is no, get the specific gaps in writing and a timeline; a vague no is a stalled career.

title: Mentor a new hire through their first solo shift
mechanism_check: New hires fail from missing building knowledge, not missing skill: transfer the map, not just the task.
Shadowing works in one direction at a time: they watch you, then you watch them -- never both at once.
Sign-off in writing protects both of you: it proves what they demonstrated, not what you assumed.
improvised_tools: The shutoff map walk as day-one orientation
A competency checklist: the dozen jobs they must demonstrate before solo
The debrief habit: after every job, what happened, why it worked, where the stop line was
steps: Day one: walk the shutoffs, the panel rooms, and the no-go zones together.
Week one: they shadow you on full shifts; narrate the why, not just the what.
Week two: they lead, you shadow; intervene only on safety, then debrief.
Debrief every job: what they did, why it worked, where they would stop next time.
Sign off competencies in writing as demonstrated; keep the checklist in their file.
stop_conditions: Never sign off a competency they have not demonstrated -- your signature is your word.
Never leave them truly solo on life-safety or high-risk work until signed off.
If they are not progressing after fair training, say so to supervision early; silent struggling helps no one.

title: Turn your shift notes into a shop SOP
mechanism_check: The shop's knowledge lives in heads; an SOP moves it into the institution where it survives turnover.
Pick the job everyone does differently: that variance is where the SOP pays for itself.
One page that gets used beats ten pages that get filed.
improvised_tools: Your own shift notes as the raw material
Photos of each step taken on a real job, not staged
One other tech as the test reader -- if they cannot follow it, rewrite it
steps: Pick the job with the most variance: the one every tech does a different way.
Write the steps you actually take, in order, with the tools you actually use.
Add the photos and the stop conditions -- the SOP is incomplete without the lines.
Have another tech follow it on a real job; fix what confuses them.
File it where the next hire will find it: the shop binder and the shared drive, both.
stop_conditions: An SOP nobody follows is clutter: if the crew will not use it, find out why and fix the SOP, not the crew.
Never write an SOP that contradicts manufacturer instructions or code -- the SOP documents compliance, it does not override it.
Review SOPs yearly; buildings change and stale procedures become hazards.

title: Design an on-call rotation that does not burn people out
mechanism_check: On-call fails from unfairness, not from calls: the same person always getting weekends will quit, and then everyone is on call.
Define what counts as a call: half of burnout is 2am calls for things that could wait until morning.
Fairness is designed: rotation, caps, and swaps on paper, not in someone's head.
improvised_tools: A written call criteria list: what pages, what waits for morning
A visible rotation calendar everyone can see and swap on
The monthly call log review: who got hit, how often, and whether the criteria held
steps: Write the call criteria: safety, water, power, security -- and explicitly what waits for morning.
Rotate weekly, not nightly; cap consecutive weeks per person.
Publish the calendar; build a simple swap rule (find your own cover, notify the lead).
Compensate the standby time fairly per policy; unpaid on-call is a retention leak.
Review the call log monthly with the crew and adjust the criteria.
stop_conditions: Never punish someone for calling in the backup -- the backup exists to be used.
A rotation everyone dreads is a retention problem: redesign it rather than lecturing about toughness.
If call volume exceeds what the rotation can absorb, escalate the staffing gap -- the rotation cannot fix understaffing.

title: Run an after-action review after a bad night
mechanism_check: The learning from a bad night is perishable: 20 minutes within 48 hours captures what a month later cannot.
Timeline first, opinions second: what happened when, before anyone says what it meant.
No-blame is not no-accountability: the review fixes systems, and systems include who was supposed to do what.
improvised_tools: A whiteboard timeline: time down the left, events across
The three questions: what worked, what did not, what changes
One owner per change, written on the board before anyone leaves
steps: Gather the crew within 48 hours; 20 minutes, standing up if you must.
Build the timeline together: what happened, in order, with times.
Ask the three questions; write every answer where all can see.
Assign one owner and one date to each change; no owner means no change.
Write it down, file it, and revisit in 30 days: did the change stick?
stop_conditions: No blame in the room: blame kills the next review, and the next bad night needs the learning more than it needs a culprit.
Never skip the 30-day follow-up; a review with no follow-up is theater.
If the same failure repeats after the review, the system did not change -- escalate the fix, do not just re-review.

title: Walk a building with the fire inspector and pass
mechanism_check: Inspectors check the same list every time: exits, extinguishers, doors, alarms, storage clearances. Pre-walk their list and the visit is boring -- boring is the goal.
Ask for the checklist: most inspectors will share what they check, and asking signals good faith.
Fix the findable before they arrive; disclose the plan for what you cannot fix yet.
improvised_tools: The inspector's checklist, requested in advance
An exit-sign battery tester and a pencil for the door-gap check (a pencil should not pass under a fire door)
Your pre-walk log with dates: proof of diligence, not just compliance
steps: Test every exit sign on battery; replace dead lamps and batteries now.
Check extinguishers: charged, tagged within the year, accessible, correct type for the hazard.
Test fire doors: they must close fully and latch on their own, every time.
Clear corridors and verify 18 inches of clearance below sprinkler heads in storage areas.
Check the alarm panel for troubles and verify the monitoring company has the current contact list.
Document the pre-walk; walk with the inspector, take notes, and ask questions.
stop_conditions: Never hide a deficiency from an inspector: fix it or disclose the correction plan with a date.
Never prop a fire door for convenience (NFPA 80) -- a propped fire door is a violation and a liability.
Never silence or reset a trouble on a fire alarm panel yourself; report it to the alarm contractor and log it.

title: Contain a sewage backup and protect the clean areas
mechanism_check: Sewage is a biohazard, not just water: containment beats cleanup, and PPE is not optional.
Protect the clean areas first: close doors, tape gaps, shut down HVAC serving the affected zone if you can do it safely.
One vac for sewage, forever: cross-contamination from a shared vac spreads the hazard.
improvised_tools: Full PPE: gloves, boots, eye protection, and a mask for aerosolized work
Barriers and tape to seal the affected area from clean zones
A wet vac designated sewage-only, plus disinfectant rated for the job
steps: Stop the source if you can do it safely; if not, contain first and call for help.
Barrier the area: tape the doors, post signs, keep occupants out.
Protect adjacent clean rooms: close doors, tape the gaps, consider shutting the zone's air handling.
Remove bulk water with the sewage-designated vac; disinfect all contacted surfaces.
Ventilate, verify the line is clear before reopening fixtures, and document everything for the report.
stop_conditions: Sewage in a food-prep or patient-care area: notify supervision immediately and consider evacuating the space -- that decision is above the tech level.
Never use the sewage vac for clean water afterward; it is sewage equipment for life.
If you do not have proper PPE, do not enter: contain from outside and wait for equipped help.

title: Shepherd a capital repair through the bureaucracy
mechanism_check: Capital money moves on paper in a fixed order: scope, quotes, justification, signatures. Skip a step and the packet comes back.
Justification speaks three languages: risk (what fails), cost of delay (what it costs later), and lifecycle (why now beats next year).
The budget owner is not your enemy: they defend a finite pot against infinite needs; your packet must win on their terms.
improvised_tools: The three-quote packet: same scope sent to three vendors, compared line by line
The one-page justification: problem, risk, cost now vs cost later, the ask
A photo of the failing asset and its nameplate data -- specificity beats adjectives
steps: Define the scope in plain language a non-technical approver can repeat.
Get three written quotes on the identical scope; note lead times, not just prices.
Write the justification: what fails, what the failure costs, what waiting costs, why this vendor.
Find the budget owner, present the packet, and answer the lifecycle question before they ask it.
Get the signature, track the spend against the quote, and report completion with the final numbers.
stop_conditions: Never split a purchase across orders to dodge a spending threshold -- that is fraud, and it is discoverable.
Never sign a contract or commitment you were not authorized to sign.
If the packet is denied, get the reason in writing; a denied capital request with a documented reason is next year's approved request.

title: Improvise within code: repairs that satisfy the inspector
mechanism_check: Improvisation has a legal ceiling, and mastery is knowing exactly where it sits for every system in your building.
The dividing line is life-safety: if the system protects lives in a fire, a medical emergency, or a power failure, your improvisation stops at documentation.
The AHJ (authority having jurisdiction) is a resource, not an adversary: when in doubt, ask before you act.
improvised_tools: The code references you actually need: NFPA 72/13/80, NEC Article 110, and your local amendments -- know which shelf they are on
The AHJ's phone number and the fire alarm contractor's number, saved where the whole crew can find them
The documentation habit: photo, log, and contractor call for everything at the line
steps: Name the system: life-safety or not. Fire alarm, sprinkler, fire pump, emergency lighting, medical gas, elevators, boilers -- all life-safety.
If life-safety: document the deficiency with photos, call the licensed contractor, log the call. Your work ends at the documentation.
If not life-safety: improvise reversibly, photograph it, log it, and schedule the permanent code-compliant repair.
Pre-walk your own work like the inspector will: clearances, labels, access, ratings.
Close the loop: verify the contractor's repair, keep the report, file it with the inspection records.
stop_conditions: THE LINE -- never improvise on: fire alarm or suppression (NFPA 72/13), medical gas (NFPA 99), elevators, boilers and pressure vessels, or electrical panel interiors.
Never defeat a safety device: interlocks, GFCIs, pressure relief valves, and door closers on rated doors stay functional.
When in doubt whether a system is life-safety, treat it as life-safety and ask the AHJ -- guessing wrong is the career-ending move.

title: Run incident command for a facilities emergency
mechanism_check: Emergencies need one voice: incident command is that voice with a structure, borrowed from fire service and scaled to facilities.
Span of control: nobody effectively runs more than five people; beyond that, add a layer.
Command is announced out loud: 'I have command' ends the argument about who is in charge before it starts.
improvised_tools: Role vests or armbands from the emergency kit: COMMAND, OPERATIONS, LOGISTICS, COMMS -- visible authority calms chaos
A command board: objectives, assignments, and a personnel accountability list
A dedicated comms channel or runner so command is never also the messenger
steps: Establish command: say it out loud, put on the identifier, pick a command post upwind and uphill of the problem.
Set the objectives in priority order: life safety, incident stabilization, property conservation.
Assign roles: operations runs the work, logistics feeds it people and parts, comms handles the building and the bosses.
Brief in cycles: short, regular updates; every assignment has an owner and a check-back time.
Track personnel: who is where, doing what. Accountability is continuous, not a headcount at the end.
Demobilize deliberately: stand down in order, debrief while it is fresh, and hand the scene back cleanly.
stop_conditions: Freelancing kills: everyone works the plan or checks in with command -- no solo heroes in an incident.
If you lose accountability of your people, stop operations and do a headcount before anything else.
When the incident exceeds facilities scope (structural, hazmat, criminal), command transfers to the professionals -- your job becomes support, and you say so out loud.

title: Build the shop's spare-parts bible
mechanism_check: The bible turns tribal knowledge into an institutional asset: what part, where it goes, where to get it, how long it takes.
It must work at 2am for the on-call tech who has never seen this failure: photo, location, and part number, no folklore.
A bible nobody updates rots: quarterly review is part of the build, not an afterthought.
improvised_tools: A shared binder plus a shared digital copy -- paper survives dead phones, digital survives lost binders
Phone photos of every stocked part next to its label
Vendor list with lead times: the part you cannot get in 48 hours is a planning problem, not a stocking one
steps: Inventory what the shop actually stocks; photograph and label each part with its real name and number.
Record where each part goes: equipment name, location, and the failure it fixes.
Note the source and lead time for each: vendor, part number, and how long reordering takes.
Organize by system (plumbing, electrical, HVAC, doors/hardware), not by where it sits on the shelf.
Place copies where the on-call tech can reach them at 2am; review and update quarterly.
stop_conditions: Never list a workaround as the approved part: the bible documents the right fix, not the clever one.
Keep safety devices sourced new and say so in the bible -- no donor safeties, ever.
If a part's lead time exceeds your critical-spares threshold, flag it to supervision: the bible reveals gaps, it does not hide them.

title: Train your replacement
mechanism_check: The final career skill is making yourself replaceable: that is how you get promoted out instead of stuck in place.
What you hand over is three things: the routes (where everything is), the relationships (who signs, who knows), and the judgment (where the lines are).
Hoarded knowledge reads as insecurity to the people deciding your next move.
improvised_tools: Your documented routes, maps, and contacts -- the real ones, including the cell numbers
A final walk-through: every shutoff, every panel, every no-go zone, narrated
Introductions, not just names: walk them to the signers, the vendors, the occupants who matter
steps: Document your routes and relationships: the map, the contacts, the unwritten rules.
Hand over the shutoff map and walk it together one last time.
Introduce them to your network in person: the budget owners, the contractors, the key occupants.
Let them run a full week while you watch and debrief; resist the urge to grab the wrench.
Step back completely; be available for questions, not for rescue.
stop_conditions: Never hoard knowledge as job security -- it blocks your own advancement and strands your team.
Never badmouth the institution to your replacement; hand them a fair start.
If they are not ready after fair training, say so honestly to supervision rather than signing off and hoping.

title: Negotiate with a vendor who owns you by contract
mechanism_check: The contract is leverage both ways: it binds them to performance standards as surely as it binds you to the vendor.
Vendors respond to documented patterns, not to frustration: dates, SLA misses, and costs move them; anger does not.
Know the renewal date: leverage peaks before renewal and vanishes after signing.
improvised_tools: The contract itself: SLA terms, response times, remedies, and the renewal date -- read before the meeting
A miss log: every late response and failed fix, dated and ticketed
The cost math: what their misses cost the institution in downtime and rework
steps: Read the SLA and the renewal date; know exactly what they promised.
Build the miss log from tickets: dates, response times vs promised, repeat failures.
Quantify the cost of the misses in downtime, not just annoyance.
Meet with facts, not frustration: present the pattern, name the SLA clause, ask for the remedy the contract provides.
Put every agreement in writing; verbal promises on contract disputes do not exist.
stop_conditions: Never threaten to break a contract you have not read -- you may be threatening to breach your own obligations.
Never accept a verbal promise on a contract dispute: writing or it did not happen.
If the vendor is the only qualified source (elevators, fire systems), negotiate the relationship, not the exit -- you need them functional.

title: Lead a multi-trade repair with one borrowed morning
mechanism_check: Borrowed time from other trades is spent in sequence, not in parallel: plan the order and the morning works; improvise the order and it does not.
Upstream first: the electrician before the drywaller, the plumber before the tile setter. Every trade verifies before the next begins.
You are the coordinator, not the boss of other trades: respect buys more morning than authority does.
improvised_tools: A one-page sequence plan: trade, task, verify, next -- shared with everyone before the morning starts
All parts staged before anyone arrives; a missing part burns borrowed time fastest
15-minute check-ins: short enough to catch drift, long enough to let people work
steps: Define the done state in one sentence everyone agrees on.
Sequence the trades upstream-first; write the order on the one-pager.
Stage every part and tool before the first trade arrives.
Run 15-minute check-ins; verify each trade's work before the next starts.
Close the loop: test the whole system, thank each trade by name, and report completion to the requester.
stop_conditions: Never let two trades work the same system simultaneously without coordination -- that is how wires get cut and pipes get punctured.
If a trade's work fails verification, stop the sequence and fix it; never build the next trade on a bad base.
If the morning runs out, demobilize cleanly and re-book rather than rushing the last trade -- rushed finish work fails first.

title: Commission a repaired system so it stays fixed
mechanism_check: A repair is not done when it works once: it is done when proven under real load, checked against adjacent systems, and documented.
'Seems fine' is how callbacks are born; commissioning is what separates a fix from a repair.
The follow-up check is part of the repair, scheduled before you leave.
improvised_tools: The system's full cycle as the test: run it the way occupants run it, twice
Your senses plus a thermometer and a tester: verify, do not assume
A follow-up date on the ticket before you close it
steps: Run the system through its full operating cycle twice, not once.
Test under real load: the flush valve with the building awake, the HVAC at occupied setpoint.
Verify nothing adjacent broke: the repair next door is the classic callback.
Photograph the finished state; update the ticket with parts used and readings taken.
Schedule the follow-up check and close the ticket only on verified performance.
stop_conditions: Never sign off a repair you did not test under load.
Never close the ticket on 'seems fine' -- verify or leave it open.
If commissioning reveals the real problem was upstream, reopen the diagnosis rather than defending the repair.

title: Handle an elevator entrapment as facilities, not the mechanic
mechanism_check: Your job is communication and calm, not the hoistway: the elevator mechanic and the fire department own the rescue.
Voice contact is the lifeline: passengers who can hear a calm human stay calm humans.
Your building's protocol decides who you call first -- know it before the entrapment, not during.
improvised_tools: The elevator emergency phone or intercom -- test that you know how it works before you need it
The contractor's emergency number and your building's entrapment protocol, posted at the security desk
A calm script: who you are, help is coming, stay seated, do not force the doors
steps: Establish voice contact with the passengers immediately; get names and any medical needs.
Reassure with specifics: who you are, who is coming, and that the car is the safest place to wait.
Call the elevator contractor AND 911/fire per your building's protocol -- both, not either/or.
Keep talking to the passengers until help arrives; never leave them without voice contact.
Meet the responders at the lobby, brief them, and document everything after.
stop_conditions: THE LINE -- never attempt to open hoistway doors, never try to move the car, never let a bystander 'help' at the doors: licensed elevator mechanic or fire department only.
Never tell passengers to climb out or force the doors, even if the car is near a landing.
If a passenger reports a medical emergency, relay it to 911 immediately -- that escalates the response priority.

title: Build a compliance-aware stop-condition culture
mechanism_check: Stop conditions only work if the whole team honors them: culture is the enforcement mechanism no procedure can replace.
A team that punishes stopping will get someone hurt; a team that celebrates stopping gets the truth about near-misses.
The red lines must be written together: lines imposed from above get ignored, lines owned by the crew get defended.
improvised_tools: The team's red-lines poster, written in the crew's own words, posted in the shop
The stop phrase: a shared sentence anyone can say to halt work, no rank required ('that's past my line')
The near-miss log: celebrated stops recorded as wins, reviewed monthly
steps: Gather the crew and write the red lines together: name the systems nobody improvises past (fire, medical gas, elevators, panels, pressure vessels).
Post the lines in the shop in plain language; review them with every new hire on day one.
Practice the stop phrase until using it is boring; role-play it in the shop, not in the emergency.
Celebrate the stops: recognize the tech who stopped work at the line, publicly.
Review the lines yearly against code updates and the near-miss log; lines are living documents.
stop_conditions: A culture that penalizes a called stop will get someone hurt: never punish the stop, investigate the pressure that made it necessary.
The red lines are minimums, not targets: the line is where improvisation ends, not where judgment begins.
If leadership overrides a red line, get the override in writing and log it -- the liability trail protects the tech who was told to proceed.
